cards.title: Tokyo
cards.sub: 30 cards · ~65 min · done before you land

cards.title: The fishing village that ate the world
cards.body: In 1603 the Tokugawa shogun chose a marshy village called Edo to rule Japan from. A hundred years later it was the largest city on the planet, with a million inhabitants, twice as many as London. In 1868 the emperor moved in from Kyoto and it was renamed: Tokyo, «the eastern capital». And one odd thing worth keeping for the end: legally, Tokyo is not a city.

cards.title: The city that rebuilt itself twice in twenty-five years
cards.body: The 1923 earthquake and the fires that followed killed more than a hundred thousand people and flattened half the city. Twenty-two years later the bombing of 1945 flattened it again. That's why almost nothing in Tokyo is older than eighty years, and why nobody feels bad about knocking down a building: here the permanent thing is the city, not the houses.

cards.claim: «No law says Tokyo is the capital of Japan»
cards.body: True. Japan has no law designating a capital: Tokyo is the capital because the emperor, the government and the parliament are there, and nobody has thought it necessary to write it down. There was a «capital construction» law in 1950 and it was repealed six years later. The country's most important city is so by habit.

cards.question: How many people pass through Shinjuku station every day?
cards.explain: Three and a half million a day, the busiest station in the world with a Guinness record: more than the entire population of Madrid going in and out every day through more than 200 exits. Getting lost inside isn't your failing: it's the standard experience.

cards.title: The delay that needs a certificate
cards.body: The average delay on the bullet train between Tokyo and Osaka is under a minute, earthquakes and typhoons included. And when a commuter train arrives five minutes late, the company hands out «delay certificates» so you can justify it at work: nobody would believe you without paper. A train leaving early, on the other hand, is news — it has happened, and the company apologised publicly.

cards.title: The machines that sell everything
cards.body: Hot canned coffee in winter, soup, umbrellas, bananas, flowers: Japan has one vending machine for every thirty people, and they work at any hour in any alley because nobody breaks or robs them. They're the thermometer of a country where you can leave your laptop on the café table and go to the bathroom. Do it: nobody will touch it.

cards.question: How many vending machines are there in the whole of Japan?
cards.explain_correct: About four million, the highest density in the world. Drinks alone bring in more than two trillion yen a year, without a single shop assistant.
cards.explain_wrong: About four million — one for every thirty inhabitants, the highest density in the world. The drinks machines alone take more than two trillion yen a year.

cards.title: No tipping here, and it isn't meanness
cards.body: Leaving money on the table is seen as odd and even offensive: good service is the norm, not an extra you pay for. The waiter will run after you to return what you «left behind». Same with taxis. What does matter: take your shoes off wherever you see a step with slippers, don't eat while walking down the street, and stand in the queue painted on the platform. With that, you're no longer the tourist.

cards.title: The streets have no names
cards.body: Tokyo addresses aren't written by street but by block: district, block number and building number — and buildings were numbered in order of construction, not position. Number 3 can sit between 14 and 27. That's why the map on your phone is a necessity here and not a convenience, and why the next card exists.

cards.question: What is a «kōban», that little box with a policeman on the corner?
cards.explain: Tokyo has hundreds of these two-officer mini stations, and a good part of their job is giving directions: they keep maps of the neighbourhood and know where 3 is between 14 and 27. They're also where lost umbrellas and wallets end up — and where they genuinely get returned.

cards.title: The crossing and the dog
cards.body: At Shibuya crossing the lights stop every car at once and up to three thousand people cross diagonally on a single green: the busiest pedestrian crossing in the world, and far more orderly than it looks from above. Outside the station Hachikō is waiting, the dog who went to meet his owner every evening for nearly ten years after the owner had died. Tokyoites meet «at Hachikō». So can you.

cards.claim: «In Tokyo you can smoke while walking down the street»
cards.body: The opposite of what you'd expect: the street is where you can't. Many wards have banned it since 2002, with fines, and smoking is only allowed in marked areas. Until recently, on the other hand, you could smoke inside bars and restaurants without any trouble. Every culture chooses where smoke is a nuisance; this one chose other people's premises over the pavement.

cards.title: The smoke that heals and the bad luck you tie up
cards.body: Sensō-ji, in Asakusa, is Tokyo's oldest temple: legend dates it to the year 645, when two fishermen pulled a tiny statue out of the river. In front there's a cauldron of incense: people scoop the smoke over themselves with their hands, towards whatever part of the body hurts. And for a hundred yen you draw an «omikuji», your fortune on a slip of paper. If it's bad, you tie it to a rack and leave it there: bad luck doesn't travel.

cards.title: The forest designed to look wild
cards.body: The forest around the Meiji shrine, right in the centre, didn't exist a century ago. In 1920 it was planted with a hundred thousand trees donated from all over Japan, following a 150-year plan: which species would grow first, which would replace them, how it would end up looking as if nobody had ever touched it. It's halfway through the plan and already fools everyone. It's the biggest silence in Tokyo.

cards.question: How many million people live in Greater Tokyo, city and metropolitan area?
cards.explain_correct: About 37 million: the largest metropolitan area in the world, as many people as the whole of Poland. And it works.
cards.explain_wrong: About 37 million — the largest metropolitan area on the planet, as many inhabitants as all of Poland. And the trains run on time.

cards.question: What was sushi originally?
options: A dish of the imperial court
cards.explain: Fish buried in fermented rice for months so it wouldn't rot; the rice was thrown away. The nigiri you know — vinegared rice with raw fish on top — was invented in Edo around 1820 as street-stall fast food, to be eaten standing up and by hand. That's still the correct way to eat it.

cards.title: The corner shop that solves everything
cards.body: A «konbini» — 7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart — is open 24 hours and sells real food: freshly made onigiri, salads, decent coffee, and you can withdraw cash, pay bills, print and collect parcels. Japan has more 7-Elevens than the United States, the country that invented them. If you don't know where to have dinner, the answer is better than it sounds: you eat well at a konbini.

cards.title: The three-million-dollar tuna
cards.body: At the New Year auction of Tokyo's fish market, a 278-kilo bluefin tuna sold in 2019 for 333 million yen, about three million dollars: the most expensive fish in history, bought by a sushi businessman who knew the photo was worth more than the fish. The market moved in 2018 from Tsukiji to Toyosu; the food stalls stayed in Tsukiji, and they're worth the early start.

cards.title: The toilet that makes you ashamed to go home
cards.body: Heated seat, a jet of warm water with adjustable pressure, a dryer, and a button that plays the sound of a flush to cover your own. More than eighty per cent of Japanese homes have one, and you'll find them in stations, konbinis and temples. The panel of buttons is intimidating; the big blue one is always the one you want. Nothing will ever be the same.

cards.title: The card is money
cards.body: Buy a Suica or a Pasmo at any station machine and top it up with cash: it's your ticket for metro, train and bus — tap in and tap out, and it charges the exact fare — and it also pays at konbinis, vending machines and lockers. Without it, every trip is a fare table and a queue. With it, Tokyo is a single city.

cards.title: The tower that measures a name
cards.body: The Tokyo Skytree is 634 metres tall: the tallest tower in the world, second only to the Dubai skyscraper. The figure isn't an accident. In Japanese, numbers can be read as syllables, and 6-3-4 reads «mu-sa-shi»: Musashi, the name of the old province where Tokyo stands. The engineers could have made it taller. They preferred it to be named after the place.

cards.question: And Tokyo Tower, the orange one that looks like the Eiffel?
options: It's an exact copy of the Paris one
It was built by a French company
It's taller than the Eiffel and weighs half as much
cards.explain: It's 333 metres — thirteen more than Paris — and weighs about 4,000 tonnes against the original's 7,300: by 1958 steel was a different thing. Some of the metal came from scrapped American tanks from the Korean War. It's painted orange and white by law, for aircraft, and it still broadcasts radio.

cards.title: The castle nobody sees
cards.body: At the exact centre of Tokyo there's a green void more than a kilometre across: the Imperial Palace, built on the shogun's castle, ringed by the moat and stone walls of Edo. The emperor lives inside and you don't go in, except two days a year. Around it, a five-kilometre loop where half of Tokyo comes out to run at dusk, always anticlockwise. That's the rule.

cards.claim: «The grounds of the Imperial Palace were once worth more than all of California»
cards.body: By the calculations of the time, yes. At the peak of the Japanese bubble, around 1989, Tokyo land had soared so far that the palace's square kilometre was worth, on paper, more than the entire state of California. The bubble burst the following year and the country took twenty years to get back up. The palace is still there, never having been sold. Perhaps that's why.

cards.title: Two hundred bars in six alleys
cards.body: In Shinjuku, two minutes from the skyscrapers, Golden Gai survives: six wooden alleys with more than two hundred bars the size of a wardrobe, five or six stools each, each with its own owner and its own theme. It's what's left of the post-war black market, and it was saved from the bulldozers by sheer stubbornness of the locals. Some don't admit tourists; many do, with a small seating charge. Go into whichever has its door open.

cards.title: The weather forecast for flowers
cards.body: Every spring the news reports the «cherry blossom front»: the line of blooming that moves up the country from south to north, with a forecast date for every city. In Tokyo it's usually late March. During those days the city does «hanami»: sitting under the trees to eat and drink, with blue tarpaulins reserving spots from the morning. The blossom is brief on purpose: that's why it matters.

cards.question: From a cherry tree opening to losing its blossom, how many days pass?
cards.explain_correct: Little more than a week, and with a day of wind or rain, less. A whole culture built around something that lasts eight days: that's the idea.
cards.explain_wrong: Little more than a week — and a day of rain shortens it. A whole country organised around something that lasts eight days. That brevity is the point, not the problem.

cards.title: The monster who is a civil servant
cards.body: Godzilla was born in 1954, nine years after Hiroshima and months after a Japanese fishing boat was caught by an American nuclear test: it was the bomb with legs. It has destroyed Tokyo on screen more than thirty times. And the city has taken it well: since 2015 it's the official tourism ambassador of Shinjuku ward, residency and all — its life-size head peers over a building in the area. It roars on the hour.

cards.question: Full circle: is Tokyo a city?
options: Yes: the largest in the world
No: it's 23 wards, each with its own mayor
cards.explain: In 1943 the City of Tokyo was dissolved and merged with its prefecture into the «Tokyo Metropolis»: 23 special wards that are cities in their own right, with their own mayor and council, plus 26 other cities and a handful of islands. What you call Tokyo is an agreement between 23 neighbours. You started in a fishing village; you're landing in a city that doesn't exist.

cards.title: The city attached to nothing
cards.body: Tokyo has been flattened by fire, earth and bombs, and every time it got up without nostalgia: it tears down its houses every thirty years, has no street names, isn't the capital by law or a city by right. You've spent 30 cards watching a city turn fish into art, punctuality into religion and a monster into a civil servant. Welcome to the biggest city in the world, which doesn't exist. You're landing.
